name: The Project Economy — Foundry & Field's Runway Bet
description: A four-round, intermediate-level venture simulation set inside Foundry & Field Ltd., a 30-month-old Dublin data-and-AI product studio (EUR 2.4M trailing revenue, 14 permanent staff, a rotating freelance bench, EUR 1.3M cash, EUR 145,000 monthly burn — roughly 9 months of runway). On 3 February 2026 a scaling fintech offers the studio its largest contract ever: a EUR 1.2M, 6-month platform build with a fixed, regulation-driven go-live date that requires roughly doubling delivery capacity. Playing the founding team, you decide how to staff one project that will either save the company or sink it — and in doing so you stress-test the asset-light, project-economy thesis: that high-skilled freelancers attached to discrete projects are a driver of venture growth, not a cost of last resort. Round 1 you diagnose the capacity-vs-demand gap and project the do-nothing runway curve, distinguishing durable baseline demand from temporary surge. Round 2 — the core decision — you set the employee-vs-freelance mix across five roles, weighing each against four tests: cost per month, the commitment tail (notice and severance), ramp-up time, and whether the capability is core (own it) or contextual (rent it). Round 3 you operationalise it: capture knowledge so it does not walk out with a contractor, and phase client milestone inflows against monthly payroll so the runway never dips below zero. Round 4 a pipeline shock hits — the EUR 500k Q3 follow-on is delayed indefinitely — and you must flex the mix, convert, or hold, then stake the model on one metric for an investor. The math rewards a modelled blend that owns the core, rents the surge, prices the total cost of employment over the headline rate, phases cash against payroll, and acts on reversibility when the shock lands — and punishes the five classic errors: over-hiring permanent staff and burning the runway under five months, going all-freelance and hollowing out IP-bearing capability, picking the lower hourly rate while ignoring the notice/severance tail, assuming a profitable contract finances itself while milestones lag payroll, and refusing to flex a deliberately flexible workforce. Final KPIs track Runway (months), Delivery Confidence, Project Margin (%), and Model Conviction.
view:
3 February 2026 · Foundry & Field Ltd., Dublin · One contract too big to staff the old way

The Project Economy

You are the founding team of a Dublin product studio with EUR 1.3M cash, 14 permanent staff and ~9 months of runway. A EUR 1.2M, 6-month contract needs you to double delivery capacity on a fixed go-live date. Build the right blend of employees and freelancers, phase the cash, and prove the asset-light model — without burning the runway.

Round 1 — Diagnose capacity and runway

Your Decisions This Round

Runway discipline: 50%
Platform architect — owns the core design & go-live support (most strategic)
Senior backend engineer — durable platform capability
Data/AI specialist — contextual, specialist, build-only
Front-end engineer — surge capacity for the build push
QA / integration engineer — temporary, ends with the build
Surge team mix: 0 employee · 5 freelance
A profitable contract still kills you if payroll is monthly and the client pays late. A buffer (or a front-loaded milestone) keeps the runway curve above zero in the gap.
SHOCK — 12 March: one of the two EUR 500k Q3 follow-on deals is delayed indefinitely. The durable demand you may have hired against just got smaller. The whole point of a flexible workforce is that it flexes.
Facilitator (your seed investor)
One question matters to me: does this staffing plan extend your runway and prove your asset-light model, or does it bet the company? A freelancer's higher monthly rate can be cheaper than an employee once you price the notice, severance and idle-time tail. Own what is strategic, rent what is temporary, phase the cash against payroll — and when demand shifts, use the flexibility you paid for.
